claim: Enteroendocrine cells (EECs) are the principal chemosensors in the GI tract.
source: Enteroendocrine cells (EECs) are the principal chemosensors in the GI tract, but investigation of their role in behavior has been limited by the difficulty of selectively targeting these cells in vivo.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about EECs.

claim: Investigation of EEC role in behavior has been limited by the difficulty of selectively targeting these cells in vivo.
source: Enteroendocrine cells (EECs) are the principal chemosensors in the GI tract, but investigation of their role in behavior has been limited by the difficulty of selectively targeting these cells in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in the field in the abstract.

claim: Multiple EEC subtypes inhibit food intake.
source: We show that multiple EEC subtypes inhibit food intake but have different effects on learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Different EEC subtypes have different effects on learning.
source: We show that multiple EEC subtypes inhibit food intake but have different effects on learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 4-6.

claim: Conditioned flavor preference is driven by release of cholecystokinin.
source: Conditioned flavor preference is driven by release of cholecystokinin whereas conditioned taste aversion is mediated by serotonin and substance P.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by pharmacological experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Conditioned taste aversion is mediated by serotonin and substance P.
source: Conditioned flavor preference is driven by release of cholecystokinin whereas conditioned taste aversion is mediated by serotonin and substance P.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by pharmacological experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Positive valence signals from EECs are transmitted by vagal afferents.
source: These positive and negative valence signals are transmitted by vagal and spinal afferents, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by vagotomy and deafferentation experiments in Figure 6.

claim: Negative valence signals from EECs are transmitted by spinal afferents.
source: These positive and negative valence signals are transmitted by vagal and spinal afferents, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by vagotomy and deafferentation experiments in Figure 6.

claim: Food choices are driven by learning.
source: Although the desire to eat is innate, our food choices are driven by learning.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Food preferences change from childhood to adulthood in part because of learned associations between flavors and post-ingestive effects.
source: Thus, the foods you enjoy today are different from your preferences as a child, in part because you have learned to associate specific flavors with their post-ingestive effects (Sclafani and Ackroff, 2012; Yamamoto and Ueji, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Learning processes cause nutrient-rich foods to become more rewarding.
source: This learning process causes nutrient-rich foods to become more rewarding and toxic substances to become aversive and is critical for guiding animals to choose safe and nutritious food sources in the wild (Myers and Sclafani, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Learning processes cause toxic substances to become aversive.
source: This learning process causes nutrient-rich foods to become more rewarding and toxic substances to become aversive and is critical for guiding animals to choose safe and nutritious food sources in the wild (Myers and Sclafani, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Learning about food is critical for guiding animals to choose safe and nutritious food sources in the wild.
source: This learning process causes nutrient-rich foods to become more rewarding and toxic substances to become aversive and is critical for guiding animals to choose safe and nutritious food sources in the wild (Myers and Sclafani, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Food learning contributes to the motivational pull of energy-dense foods in modern society.
source: It also contributes to the motivational pull of energy-dense foods in modern society (Johnson et al., 1991; Kern et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The small intestine epithelium is one of the first sites of post-ingestive chemosensing.
source: One of the first sites of post-ingestive chemosensing is the epithelium of the small intestine, which contains a family of specialized sensory cells known as enteroendocrine cells (EECs) (Adriaenssens et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: EECs exist as multiple subtypes.
source: EECs exist as multiple subtypes and express receptors and transporters that allow them to monitor the chemical contents of the intestinal lumen.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by the scRNA-seq data in Figure 1.

claim: EECs express receptors and transporters that allow them to monitor the chemical contents of the intestinal lumen.
source: EECs exist as multiple subtypes and express receptors and transporters that allow them to monitor the chemical contents of the intestinal lumen.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by expression data in Figure 2.

claim: EECs release an array of hormones including CCK, GIP, GLP-1, PYY, SST, and 5-HT in response to detection of chemical cues.
source: In response to detection of chemical cues, EECs release an array of hormones that include CCK, GIP, GLP-1, PYY, SST, and 5-HT.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by expression data in Figure 1.

claim: EEC hormones can act on local sensory neurons in the lamina propria.
source: These molecules can act on local sensory neurons in the lamina propria (Bellono et al., 2017; Kaelberer et al., 2018; Latorre et al., 2016; Ye et al., 2021) or on distant organs via the circulation to modulate digestion, metabolism and appetite (Adriaenssens et al., 2018; Gribble and Reimann, 2016; Najjar et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: EEC hormones can act on distant organs via the circulation to modulate digestion, metabolism and appetite.
source: These molecules can act on local sensory neurons in the lamina propria (Bellono et al., 2017; Kaelberer et al., 2018; Latorre et al., 2016; Ye et al., 2021) or on distant organs via the circulation to modulate digestion, metabolism and appetite (Adriaenssens et al., 2018; Gribble and Reimann, 2016; Najjar et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: EECs link the detection of chemicals in the gut to the feedback regulation of behavior and physiology.
source: Thus, EECs link the detection of chemicals in the gut to the feedback regulation of behavior and physiology.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from established knowledge about EEC function.

claim: EECs are sparsely scattered throughout the intestinal epithelium at approximately 1% of cells.
source: EECs are sparsely scattered throughout the intestinal epithelium (~1% of cells), undergo rapid turnover (~1 week), and cannot be targeted with viral injections (Polyak et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: EECs undergo rapid turnover of approximately 1 week.
source: EECs are sparsely scattered throughout the intestinal epithelium (~1% of cells), undergo rapid turnover (~1 week), and cannot be targeted with viral injections (Polyak et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: EECs cannot be targeted with viral injections.
source: EECs are sparsely scattered throughout the intestinal epithelium (~1% of cells), undergo rapid turnover (~1 week), and cannot be targeted with viral injections (Polyak et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Marker genes that distinguish EEC subtypes are also broadly expressed in other tissues that regulate metabolism and appetite, including sensory neurons throughout the gut.
source: While there are marker genes that distinguish EEC subtypes from each other, these genes are also broadly expressed in other tissues that regulate metabolism and appetite, including, critically, sensory neurons throughout the gut.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation and demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The study describes a general strategy for genetic access to a spectrum of EEC subtypes in vivo.
source: Here, we describe a general strategy for genetic access to a spectrum of EEC subtypes in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution described in the introduction and demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: The intersectional genetic approach can be used to target actuators to EECs selectively relative to all other cells in the body.
source: We show that this approach can be used to target actuators to EECs selectively relative to all other cells in the body and thereby control the release of their natural cocktail of hormones at their endogenous sites in the intestine.
evidence: This is a methodological finding demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: The intersectional genetic approach can control the release of EEC hormones at their endogenous sites in the intestine.
source: We show that this approach can be used to target actuators to EECs selectively relative to all other cells in the body and thereby control the release of their natural cocktail of hormones at their endogenous sites in the intestine.
evidence: This is a methodological finding demonstrated in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The study enriched for EECs prior to sequencing by labeling all cells derived from the common EEC progenitor using Neurog3-Cre R26LSL-tdTomato mice.
source: We therefore enriched for EECs prior to sequencing by labeling all cells derived from the common EEC progenitor using Neurog3-Cre R26LSL-tdTomato mice and then sorting tdTomato+ cells from the small intestine (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a methodological approach described in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The lineage-tracing method yielded 7001 cells with 2,168 EECs for analysis.
source: This lineage-tracing method captures EECs at any stage after differentiation and yielded 7001 cells (with 2,168 EECs) for analysis.
evidence: This is a data summary from the scRNA-seq experiment.

claim: The study integrated scRNA-seq data with a complementary dataset that used a pulse-trace reporter Neurog3Chrono to transiently label EECs at an early stage after differentiation.
source: We then integrated our scRNA-seq data with a complementary dataset (2337 cells with 1244 EECs) that used a pulse-trace reporter Neurog3Chrono to transiently label EECs at an early stage after differentiation (Gehart et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological approach with citation to the source of the complementary dataset.

claim: The two datasets differentially enriched for cell types depending on the timing after differentiation.
source: These two datasets differentially enriched for cell types depending on the timing after differentiation (Figure 1A, D and E) and together provide more complete coverage of EEC subtypes than either individually.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1D and E showing different cell type distributions.

claim: The combined datasets provide more complete coverage of EEC subtypes than either individually.
source: These two datasets differentially enriched for cell types depending on the timing after differentiation (Figure 1A, D and E) and together provide more complete coverage of EEC subtypes than either individually.
evidence: This is an inference from the complementary nature of the datasets shown in Figure 1.

claim: Unsupervised clustering analysis revealed eight clusters of EECs.
source: Unsupervised clustering analysis revealed eight clusters of EECs (Figure 1B, C and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Two well-segregated clusters of enterochromaffin cells correspond to early and late-stage cells (EC1 and EC2).
source: We observed two well-segregated clusters of enterochromaffin cells that correspond to early and late-stage cells (EC1 and EC2).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1B and F.

claim: EC1 and EC2 enterochromaffin cell subtypes can be distinguished by the expression of Tph1/Tac1 or Tph1/Sct.
source: These subtypes can be distinguished by the expression of Tph1/Tac1 or Tph1/Sct but do not express any other peptide hormone (Gehart et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1F with citation to prior work.

claim: EC1 and EC2 enterochromaffin cells do not express any peptide hormone other than those that distinguish them.
source: These subtypes can be distinguished by the expression of Tph1/Tac1 or Tph1/Sct but do not express any other peptide hormone (Gehart et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1C and F with citation.

claim: Three EEC clusters share high expression of the peptide hormones Cck and Sct.
source: We also observed three EEC clusters that share high expression of the peptide hormone Cck and Sct.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1C and F.

claim: Two of the Cck/Sct-expressing clusters correspond to the canonical N/L cells (Cck/Gcg/Pyy) and I cells (CCK).
source: Two of these clusters correspond to the canonical N/L cells (Cck/Gcg/Pyy) and I cells (CCK), whereas the third uniquely co-expresses Cck and Tph1 (cluster EC/EEC).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1B, C, and F.

claim: A third Cck/Sct-expressing cluster uniquely co-expresses Cck and Tph1 (cluster EC/EEC).
source: Two of these clusters correspond to the canonical N/L cells (Cck/Gcg/Pyy) and I cells (CCK), whereas the third uniquely co-expresses Cck and Tph1 (cluster EC/EEC).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1B, C, and F.

claim: The EC/EEC population has not been reported in other recent single-cell sequencing studies.
source: This third population has not been reported in other recent single-cell sequencing studies but likely corresponds to CCK+/5-HT+ cells that have been described immunohistochemically (Reynaud et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding with citation to prior immunohistochemical work.

claim: The EC/EEC population likely corresponds to CCK+/5-HT+ cells that have been described immunohistochemically.
source: This third population has not been reported in other recent single-cell sequencing studies but likely corresponds to CCK+/5-HT+ cells that have been described immunohistochemically (Reynaud et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression patterns with citation to prior work.

claim: Well-segregated clusters of D cells (Sst), K cells (Gip), and X cells (Ghrl) were observed.
source: Finally, we observed well-segregated clusters of D cells (Sst), K cells (Gip), and X cells (Ghrl) that are consistent with previous reports (Gehart et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1B, C, and F with citation.

claim: Many canonical EEC subtypes can be differentiated from each other by expression of individual hormones (e.g. EC, D, K, and X cells).
source: Thus, many canonical EEC subtypes can be differentiated from each other by expression of individual hormones (e.g. EC, D, K, and X cells), whereas others (N/L, I, EC/EEC cells) show partially overlapping hormonal expression.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C and F.

claim: Some EEC subtypes (N/L, I, EC/EEC cells) show partially overlapping hormonal expression.
source: Thus, many canonical EEC subtypes can be differentiated from each other by expression of individual hormones (e.g. EC, D, K, and X cells), whereas others (N/L, I, EC/EEC cells) show partially overlapping hormonal expression.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C and F.

claim: Different EEC subtypes displayed unique patterns of chemoreceptor and transporter expression.
source: Different EEC subtypes displayed unique patterns of chemoreceptor and transporter expression (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The receptors Trpa1 and Olfr558 were selectively expressed in enterochromaffin cells.
source: For example, the receptors Trpa1 and Olfr558, which detect irritants and microbial metabolites, respectively, were selectively expressed in enterochromaffin cells (Bellono et al., 2017), whereas nutrient-sensing I/K/N/L cells expressed an array of receptors and transporters involved in the detection of sugars, fats, and amino acids (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2A with citation.

claim: Trpa1 detects irritants.
source: For example, the receptors Trpa1 and Olfr558, which detect irritants and microbial metabolites, respectively, were selectively expressed in enterochromaffin cells (Bellono et al., 2017), whereas nutrient-sensing I/K/N/L cells expressed an array of receptors and transporters involved in the detection of sugars, fats, and amino acids (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Olfr558 detects microbial metabolites.
source: For example, the receptors Trpa1 and Olfr558, which detect irritants and microbial metabolites, respectively, were selectively expressed in enterochromaffin cells (Bellono et al., 2017), whereas nutrient-sensing I/K/N/L cells expressed an array of receptors and transporters involved in the detection of sugars, fats, and amino acids (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Nutrient-sensing I/K/N/L cells expressed an array of receptors and transporters involved in the detection of sugars, fats, and amino acids.
source: For example, the receptors Trpa1 and Olfr558, which detect irritants and microbial metabolites, respectively, were selectively expressed in enterochromaffin cells (Bellono et al., 2017), whereas nutrient-sensing I/K/N/L cells expressed an array of receptors and transporters involved in the detection of sugars, fats, and amino acids (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CCK+ EECs were recently reported to release glutamate at synapses with sensory afferents.
source: Of note, CCK+ EECs were recently reported to release glutamate at synapses with sensory afferents, thereby enabling the rapid control of feeding behavior (Buchanan et al., 2022; Kaelberer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as prior work with citations.

claim: Glutamate release by CCK+ EECs enables the rapid control of feeding behavior.
source: Of note, CCK+ EECs were recently reported to release glutamate at synapses with sensory afferents, thereby enabling the rapid control of feeding behavior (Buchanan et al., 2022; Kaelberer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as prior work with citations.

claim: The expression of vesicular glutamate transporters (Slc17a6, Slc17a7, and Slc17a8) was not detected in any cell type within the intestinal epithelium by scRNA-Seq.
source: However, we were unable to detect the expression of vesicular glutamate transporters (Slc17a6, Slc17a7, and Slc17a8) in any cell type within the intestinal epithelium by scRNA-Seq (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The glutamate transporter Slc17a8 (VGLUT3) was detected at a low level in both tdTomato+ and tdTomato- cells in bulk RNA-seq.
source: The glutamate transporter Slc17a8 (VGLUT3) was detected at a low level in both tdTomato+ and tdTomato- cells, whereas mRNAs for Slc17a6 (VGLUT2) and Slc17a7 (VGLUT1) were not detected in any sample (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from the bulk RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: mRNAs for Slc17a6 (VGLUT2) and Slc17a7 (VGLUT1) were not detected in any bulk RNA-seq sample.
source: The glutamate transporter Slc17a8 (VGLUT3) was detected at a low level in both tdTomato+ and tdTomato- cells, whereas mRNAs for Slc17a6 (VGLUT2) and Slc17a7 (VGLUT1) were not detected in any sample (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from the bulk RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Slc17a7Cre recombination labeled primarily axons innervating the intestinal villi, consistent with VGLUT1 expression in sensory neurons.
source: Slc17a7Cre recombination labeled primarily axons innervating the intestinal villi, consistent with VGLUT1 expression in sensory neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from Cre reporter experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: For Slc17a6Cre and Slc17a8Cre, labeled cells within the villi were localized primarily to the lamina propria rather than the epithelium.
source: For Slc17a6Cre and Slc17a8Cre, we observed some labeled cells within the villi, but these were localized primarily to the lamina propria rather than the epithelium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from Cre reporter experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cells labeled by Slc17a6Cre and Slc17a8Cre appeared spherical and lacked the elongated, 'flask-shaped' morphology characteristic of open-type EECs.
source: Consistently, these tdTomato+ cells appeared spherical and lacked the elongated, 'flask-shaped' morphology characteristic of open-type EECs (Liddle, 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from Cre reporter experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with citation.

claim: Cells labeled by Slc17a6Cre and Slc17a8Cre showed no overlap with 5-HT.
source: They also showed no overlap with 5-HT, which labels all enterochromaffin cells and ~40% of CCK+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: 5-HT labels all enterochromaffin cells and approximately 40% of CCK+ cells.
source: They also showed no overlap with 5-HT, which labels all enterochromaffin cells and ~40% of CCK+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Glutamate release by EECs may be restricted to rare cells or involve novel, VGLUT-independent mechanisms for loading glutamate into synaptic vesicles.
source: This suggests that glutamate release by EECs may be restricted to rare cells or involve novel, VGLUT-independent mechanisms for loading glutamate into synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is speculation based on the lack of VGLUT expression in EECs.

claim: The Villin-Flp transgenic mouse efficiently labels the intestinal epithelium (>99%).
source: We first generated a Villin-Flp transgenic mouse that efficiently labels the intestinal epithelium (>99%).
evidence: This is a methodological finding shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The Villin-Flp line does not label other tissues, including non-epithelial cells, the nervous system, and visceral organs, with the exception of rare cells in pancreas (~1%).
source: We extensively characterized the specificity of this line to show that it does not label other tissues, including non-epithelial cells, the nervous system, and visceral organs (Figure 3B, C), with the exception of rare cells in pancreas (~1%).
evidence: This is a methodological finding shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: CckCre and Tac1Cre also label sensory and motor neurons that innervate the intestinal villi.
source: For example, CckCre and Tac1Cre, which demarcate major subclasses of EECs (discussed below), also label sensory and motor neurons that innervate the intestinal villi (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is a finding from Cre reporter experiments shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: CckCre labeling of neurons is due to widespread recombination in the enteric nervous system.
source: For CckCre, this labeling is due to widespread recombination in the enteric nervous system (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and Morarach et al., 2021) whereas Tac1Cre labels subsets of spinal, vagal, and enteric neurons (Browne et al., 2017; Kupari et al., 2019; Morarach et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C with citations.

claim: Tac1Cre labels subsets of spinal, vagal, and enteric neurons.
source: For CckCre, this labeling is due to widespread recombination in the enteric nervous system (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and Morarach et al., 2021) whereas Tac1Cre labels subsets of spinal, vagal, and enteric neurons (Browne et al., 2017; Kupari et al., 2019; Morarach et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Fev-Cre efficiently labels all EEC subtypes tested (~90% of cells) but not other cell types in the intestinal epithelium.
source: Among EEC progenitor markers, we found that Fev-Cre efficiently labels all EEC subtypes tested (~90% of cells) but not other cell types in the intestinal epithelium (Figure 3H, I, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: Fev-Cre enables targeting all EECs simultaneously.
source: Thus, this line enables targeting all EECs simultaneously.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that Fev-Cre labels all EEC subtypes.

claim: Neurog3-Cre and Isl1Cre labeled other epithelial cells or the stem cell niche and therefore lacked useful specificity.
source: In contrast, the progenitor markers Neurog3-Cre and Isl1Cre labeled other epithelial cells (Figure 1B) or the stem cell niche (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and therefore lacked useful specificity.
evidence: This is a finding from reporter experiments shown in Figure 1B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tac1Cre, CckCre, and SstCre label distinct EEC subsets.
source: We also tested Cre drivers corresponding to EEC peptide hormones, which revealed that Tac1Cre, CckCre, and SstCre label distinct EEC subsets (Figure 3H, I, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: Tac1Cre specifically and efficiently labels 5-HT producing enterochromaffin cells, including both early stage (TAC1+, cluster EC.1) and late stage (which have lost TAC1 expression, cluster EC.2) cells.
source: Tac1Cre specifically and efficiently labels 5-HT producing enterochromaffin cells, including both early stage (TAC1+, cluster EC.1) and late stage (which have lost TAC1 expression, cluster EC.2) cells but not EECs that express the peptides CCK, GLP-1, GIP, or SST.
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: Tac1Cre does not label EECs that express the peptides CCK, GLP-1, GIP, or SST.
source: Tac1Cre specifically and efficiently labels 5-HT producing enterochromaffin cells, including both early stage (TAC1+, cluster EC.1) and late stage (which have lost TAC1 expression, cluster EC.2) cells but not EECs that express the peptides CCK, GLP-1, GIP, or SST.
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: CckCre labels virtually all CCK+ cells (~98% in villi).
source: On the other hand, CckCre labels virtually all CCK+ cells (~98% in villi) and majority of GLP-1 and GIP expressing cells, consistent with our scRNA-seq data (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3I.

claim: CckCre labels the majority of GLP-1 and GIP expressing cells.
source: On the other hand, CckCre labels virtually all CCK+ cells (~98% in villi) and majority of GLP-1 and GIP expressing cells, consistent with our scRNA-seq data (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3I, consistent with scRNA-seq data.

claim: Subsets of CckCre labeled EECs also co-express 5-HT.
source: Interestingly, we found that subsets of CckCre labeled EECs also co-express 5-HT (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3H.

claim: 5-HT+ cells labeled by CckCre are distinct from the 5-HT cells derived from the TAC1+ lineage and likely correspond to cluster EC/EEC.
source: These cells are distinct from the 5-HT cells derived from the TAC1 + lineage and likely correspond to cluster EC/EEC in our scRNA-seq data (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is an inference based on immunohistochemistry and scRNA-seq data.

claim: GcgCre shows a similar recombination pattern to CckCre.
source: A similar recombination pattern to CckCre was observed for GcgCre.
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3I.

claim: SstCre specifically targets D cells (SST+) without any labeling of other cell types.
source: Finally, SstCre specifically targets D cells (SST+) without any labeling of other cell types.
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: CNO activation of all EECs (labeled by Fev-Cre) caused a robust reduction of food intake in fasted mice.
source: We found that CNO activation of all EECs (labeled by Fev-Cre) caused a robust reduction of food intake in fasted mice, whereas CNO alone had no effect in littermate controls (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from chemogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: CNO alone had no effect on food intake in littermate controls.
source: We found that CNO activation of all EECs (labeled by Fev-Cre) caused a robust reduction of food intake in fasted mice, whereas CNO alone had no effect in littermate controls (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is a control finding from chemogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Tac1Cre cells (enterochromaffin cells) are sufficient to inhibit food intake when activated individually.
source: We further showed that several EEC subtypes were sufficient to inhibit food intake when activated individually, including Tac1Cre cells (enterochromaffin cells) as well as CckCre and GcgCre cells (I/NL/K cells) (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from chemogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: CckCre cells are sufficient to inhibit food intake when activated individually.
source: We further showed that several EEC subtypes were sufficient to inhibit food intake when activated individually, including Tac1Cre cells (enterochromaffin cells) as well as CckCre and GcgCre cells (I/NL/K cells) (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from chemogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: GcgCre cells are sufficient to inhibit food intake when activated individually.
source: We further showed that several EEC subtypes were sufficient to inhibit food intake when activated individually, including Tac1Cre cells (enterochromaffin cells) as well as CckCre and GcgCre cells (I/NL/K cells) (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from chemogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: There was no effect on food intake following stimulation of SstCre cells (D cells).
source: In contrast, there was no effect on food intake following stimulation of SstCre cells (D cells; Figure 4B, C) or X cells that express ghrelin (via GhrlCre; R26LSL-hM3D mice; Figure 4B-D).
evidence: This is a finding from chemogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: There was no effect on food intake following stimulation of X cells that express ghrelin.
source: In contrast, there was no effect on food intake following stimulation of SstCre cells (D cells; Figure 4B, C) or X cells that express ghrelin (via GhrlCre; R26LSL-hM3D mice; Figure 4B-D).
evidence: This is a finding from chemogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: The lack of response in X cells may reflect the fact that ghrelin stimulates feeding only when administered at supraphysiologic levels (~20-fold above baseline).
source: The lack of response in X cells may reflect the fact that ghrelin stimulates feeding only when administered at supraphysiologic levels (~20-fold above baseline, McFarlane et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation based on prior work cited.

claim: Activation of all intestinal EECs labeled by Fev-Cre induced dramatic aversion, such that animals avoided consumption of sucrose after just one training session.
source: We found that activation of all intestinal EECs labeled by Fev-Cre induced dramatic aversion, such that animals avoided consumption of sucrose after just one training session (Figure 4F) and completely reversed their preference in a subsequent two-bottle test (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from CTA experiments shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Activation of all intestinal EECs labeled by Fev-Cre completely reversed sucrose preference in a subsequent two-bottle test.
source: We found that activation of all intestinal EECs labeled by Fev-Cre induced dramatic aversion, such that animals avoided consumption of sucrose after just one training session (Figure 4F) and completely reversed their preference in a subsequent two-bottle test (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from CTA experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: CTA learning was absent in littermate controls (lacking hM3D expression) treated with CNO.
source: This learning was absent in littermate controls (lacking hM3D expression) treated with CNO (Figure 4F-G).
evidence: This is a control finding from CTA experiments shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Activation of Tac1Cre-labeled enterochromaffin cells alone was sufficient to drive CTA.
source: Testing of individual subtypes revealed that activation of Tac1Cre-labeled enterochromaffin cells alone was sufficient to drive this CTA, whereas activation of other subtypes (labeled by CckCre, GcgCre, or SstCre) created no measurable aversion (Figure 4F-G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from CTA experiments shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Activation of EEC subtypes labeled by CckCre, GcgCre, or SstCre created no measurable aversion in CTA assays.
source: Testing of individual subtypes revealed that activation of Tac1Cre-labeled enterochromaffin cells alone was sufficient to drive this CTA, whereas activation of other subtypes (labeled by CckCre, GcgCre, or SstCre) created no measurable aversion (Figure 4F-G).
evidence: This is a finding from CTA experiments shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Activation of EECs labeled by CckCre was sufficient to induce robust conditioned flavor preference.
source: This revealed that activation of EECs labeled by CckCre or GcgCre was sufficient to induce robust conditioned preference (Figure 4I), whereas activation of D cells labeled by SstCre had no effect (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from CFP experiments shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Activation of EECs labeled by GcgCre was sufficient to induce robust conditioned flavor preference.
source: This revealed that activation of EECs labeled by CckCre or GcgCre was sufficient to induce robust conditioned preference (Figure 4I), whereas activation of D cells labeled by SstCre had no effect (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from CFP experiments shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Activation of D cells labeled by SstCre had no effect on conditioned flavor preference.
source: This revealed that activation of EECs labeled by CckCre or GcgCre was sufficient to induce robust conditioned preference (Figure 4I), whereas activation of D cells labeled by SstCre had no effect (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a finding from CFP experiments shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Tac1Cre labels enterochromaffin cells that release 5-HT, substance P (encoded by the Tac1 gene), and PYY.
source: Tac1Cre labels enterochromaffin cells that release 5-HT, substance P (encoded by the Tac1 gene), and PYY, while CckCre labels EECs that release CCK, GLP-1, GIP, PYY, and 5-HT (Figure 3H, I, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: CckCre labels EECs that release CCK, GLP-1, GIP, PYY, and 5-HT.
source: Tac1Cre labels enterochromaffin cells that release 5-HT, substance P (encoded by the Tac1 gene), and PYY, while CckCre labels EECs that release CCK, GLP-1, GIP, PYY, and 5-HT (Figure 3H, I, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: The acute inhibition of feeding caused by enterochromaffin cell stimulation (Tac1Cre) was attenuated by treatment with an antagonist targeting 5-HT3R but not TACR1 or NPY2R.
source: We found that the acute inhibition of feeding caused by enterochromaffin cell stimulation (Tac1Cre) was attenuated by treatment with an antagonist targeting 5-HT3R but not TACR1 or NPY2R (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A 5-HT3R antagonist had no effect on the inhibition of feeding caused by CckCre EECs.
source: Interestingly, although 40% of CckCre EECs also secrete 5-HT (Figure 3I), a 5-HT3R antagonist had no effect on the inhibition of feeding caused by CckCre EECs.
evidence: This is a finding from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The feeding inhibition caused by CckCre cells was fully blocked by antagonists against either CCKAR or NPY2R, but not TACR1 or GLP1R.
source: In contrast, this feeding inhibition was fully blocked by antagonists against either CCKAR or NPY2R, but not TACR1 or GLP1R (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The same gut hormone can have different effects when released by different cell types.
source: Thus, although the hormones released by Tac1Cre EECs and CckCre EECs are partially overlapping, the receptors required for their acute inhibition of feeding are different (5-HT3R for Tac1Cre EECs, versus CCKAR and NPY2R for CckCre EECs) (Figure 5E). This suggests that the same gut hormone can have different effects when released by different cell types.
evidence: This is an inference from the pharmacological data showing different receptor requirements.

claim: Inhibition of 5-HT3R or TACR1 during training could partially block the CTA induced by enterochromaffin cell activation.
source: We found that inhibition of 5-HT3R or TACR1 during training could partially block the CTA induced by enterochromaffin cell activation, whereas the NPY2R antagonist had no effect (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pharmacological experiments during CTA training shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The NPY2R antagonist had no effect on CTA induced by enterochromaffin cell activation.
source: We found that inhibition of 5-HT3R or TACR1 during training could partially block the CTA induced by enterochromaffin cell activation, whereas the NPY2R antagonist had no effect (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from pharmacological experiments during CTA training shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Combined treatment with 5-HT3R and TACR1 antagonists during training abolished the enterochromaffin cell induced CTA.
source: Strikingly, combined treatment with 5-HT3R and TACR1 antagonists during training abolished the enterochromaffin cell induced CTA (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pharmacological experiments during CTA training shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Enterochromaffin cells can induce learned aversion by signaling through the 5-HT3R and TAC1R.
source: Thus, enterochromaffin cells can induce learned aversion by signaling through the 5-HT3R and TAC1R, whereas their acute inhibition of feeding requires only 5-HT/5-HT3R signals (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a summary inference from the pharmacological data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Enterochromaffin cell acute inhibition of feeding requires only 5-HT/5-HT3R signals.
source: Thus, enterochromaffin cells can induce learned aversion by signaling through the 5-HT3R and TAC1R, whereas their acute inhibition of feeding requires only 5-HT/5-HT3R signals (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a summary inference from the pharmacological data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Flavor preference induced by CckCre cell stimulation was prevented by blocking CCKAR but not NPY2R.
source: We found that flavor preference induced by CckCre cell stimulation was prevented by blocking CCKAR but not NPY2R (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pharmacological experiments during CFP training shown in Figure 5D.

claim: NPY2R antagonists can block CckCre-induced satiety, but not flavor preference.
source: The fact that NPY2R antagonists can block CckCre-induced satiety, but not flavor preference, reveals these cells influence satiety and learning through separable mechanisms (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an inference from the differential effects of NPY2R antagonists shown in Figure 5.

claim: CckCre cells influence satiety and learning through separable mechanisms.
source: The fact that NPY2R antagonists can block CckCre-induced satiety, but not flavor preference, reveals these cells influence satiety and learning through separable mechanisms (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an inference from the differential effects of NPY2R antagonists shown in Figure 5.

claim: Vagal and spinal afferents comprise the two major ascending circuits for gut-brain communication.
source: Vagal and spinal afferents comprise the two major ascending circuits for gut-brain communication (Brookes et al., 2013; Latorre et al., 2016), and subsets of these sensory neurons express receptors for hormones released by EECs, including 5-HT3R, CCKAR, and NPY2R (Bai et al., 2019; Li et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Subsets of vagal and spinal sensory neurons express receptors for hormones released by EECs, including 5-HT3R, CCKAR, and NPY2R.
source: Vagal and spinal afferents comprise the two major ascending circuits for gut-brain communication (Brookes et al., 2013; Latorre et al., 2016), and subsets of these sensory neurons express receptors for hormones released by EECs, including 5-HT3R, CCKAR, and NPY2R (Bai et al., 2019; Li et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Vagotomy abolished the feeding inhibition induced by activation of CckCre labeled EECs.
source: We found that vagotomy abolished the feeding inhibition induced by activation of CckCre labeled EECs (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F) but had no effect on the reduction in feeding induced by Tac1Cre EECs (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from vagotomy experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Vagotomy had no effect on the reduction in feeding induced by Tac1Cre EECs.
source: We found that vagotomy abolished the feeding inhibition induced by activation of CckCre labeled EECs (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F) but had no effect on the reduction in feeding induced by Tac1Cre EECs (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from vagotomy experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Intrathecal RTX treatment abolished the feeding inhibition induced by the Tac1Cre labeled EECs.
source: In contrast, intrathecal RTX treatment abolished the feeding inhibition induced by the Tac1Cre labeled EECs (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G) but had no effect on responses to CckCre EECs (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RTX deafferentation experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Intrathecal RTX treatment had no effect on responses to CckCre EECs.
source: In contrast, intrathecal RTX treatment abolished the feeding inhibition induced by the Tac1Cre labeled EECs (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G) but had no effect on responses to CckCre EECs (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is a finding from RTX deafferentation experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The EECs labeled by Tac1Cre inhibit food intake via spinal pathways.
source: Thus, the EECs labeled by Tac1Cre and CckCre inhibit food intake via spinal and vagal pathways, respectively (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a summary inference from the vagotomy and RTX experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The EECs labeled by CckCre inhibit food intake via vagal pathways.
source: Thus, the EECs labeled by Tac1Cre and CckCre inhibit food intake via spinal and vagal pathways, respectively (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a summary inference from the vagotomy and RTX experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Intrathecal RTX prior to training was sufficient to partially prevent the acquisition of CTA following Tac1Cre activation.
source: Intrathecal RTX prior to training was sufficient to partially prevent the acquisition of CTA following Tac1Cre activation, indicating that spinal afferents contribute to this process (Figure 6F), whereas vagotomy prior to training did not block this CTA (as reflected by the reduction in sucrose intake after one round of training; Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RTX experiments during CTA training shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Spinal afferents contribute to CTA induced by Tac1Cre activation.
source: Intrathecal RTX prior to training was sufficient to partially prevent the acquisition of CTA following Tac1Cre activation, indicating that spinal afferents contribute to this process (Figure 6F), whereas vagotomy prior to training did not block this CTA (as reflected by the reduction in sucrose intake after one round of training; Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is an inference from the RTX experiments shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Vagotomy prior to training did not block CTA induced by Tac1Cre activation.
source: Intrathecal RTX prior to training was sufficient to partially prevent the acquisition of CTA following Tac1Cre activation, indicating that spinal afferents contribute to this process (Figure 6F), whereas vagotomy prior to training did not block this CTA (as reflected by the reduction in sucrose intake after one round of training; Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is a finding from vagotomy experiments during CTA training shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The conditioned flavor preference induced by the CckCre activation was unaffected by the ablation of TRPV1+ spinal afferents.
source: In contrast, the conditioned flavor preference induced by the CckCre activation was unaffected by the ablation of TRPV1 +spinal afferents but abolished by vagotomy (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a finding from RTX experiments during CFP training shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The conditioned flavor preference induced by the CckCre activation was abolished by vagotomy.
source: In contrast, the conditioned flavor preference induced by the CckCre activation was unaffected by the ablation of TRPV1 +spinal afferents but abolished by vagotomy (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from vagotomy experiments during CFP training shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Vagal afferents are necessary for the CckCre EECs to transmit positive valence to the brain.
source: Thus, vagal afferents are necessary for the CckCre EECs to transmit positive valence to the brain, whereas enterochromaffin-cell-mediated aversion is relayed at least in part by spinal pathways (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a summary inference from the vagotomy and RTX experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Enterochromaffin-cell-mediated aversion is relayed at least in part by spinal pathways.
source: Thus, vagal afferents are necessary for the CckCre EECs to transmit positive valence to the brain, whereas enterochromaffin-cell-mediated aversion is relayed at least in part by spinal pathways (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a summary inference from the vagotomy and RTX experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Direct tests of EEC function have been limited by the difficulty of selectively accessing these cells for manipulations in vivo.
source: However, direct tests of their function have been limited by the difficulty of selectively accessing these cells for manipulations in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in the field in the discussion.

claim: One recent study used the gene Insl5 to target GLP1/PYY+ EECs in the colon.
source: One recent study used the gene Insl5 to target GLP1/PYY+ EECs in the colon (Lewis et al., 2020), but most marker genes that label EEC subtypes are broadly expressed in other tissues important for metabolism and appetite (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Most marker genes that label EEC subtypes are broadly expressed in other tissues important for metabolism and appetite.
source: One recent study used the gene Insl5 to target GLP1/PYY+ EECs in the colon (Lewis et al., 2020), but most marker genes that label EEC subtypes are broadly expressed in other tissues important for metabolism and appetite (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation and demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The intersectional approach uses Flp and Cre drivers as sequential selectivity filters to progressively restrict transgene expression to the intestinal epithelium and then to cell types within that structure.
source: This approach uses Flp and Cre drivers as sequential selectivity filters to progressively restrict transgene expression to the intestinal epithelium and then to cell types within that structure.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: The intersectional approach makes it possible to target rare EEC subsets (each <1% of epithelial cells) with high efficiency (>90% labeling) and undetectable recombination in off-target tissues.
source: This makes it possible to target rare EEC subsets (each <1% of epithelial cells) with high efficiency (>90% labeling) and undetectable recombination in off-target tissues.
evidence: This is a summary of the methodological findings demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: All EECs express more than one hormone.
source: While much has been learned from this pioneering work, all EECs express more than one hormone (Fothergill and Furness, 2018; Grunddal et al., 2016; Habib et al., 2012; Sykaras et al., 2014), and these hormone cocktails are not released directly into blood but rather into the lamina propria in the vicinity of the axons of vagal and spinal afferents (Latorre et al., 2016; Najjar et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: EEC hormone cocktails are not released directly into blood but rather into the lamina propria in the vicinity of the axons of vagal and spinal afferents.
source: While much has been learned from this pioneering work, all EECs express more than one hormone (Fothergill and Furness, 2018; Grunddal et al., 2016; Habib et al., 2012; Sykaras et al., 2014), and these hormone cocktails are not released directly into blood but rather into the lamina propria in the vicinity of the axons of vagal and spinal afferents (Latorre et al., 2016; Najjar et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Some EECs likely form direct synaptic connections with vagal and spinal afferent terminals.
source: Some EECs likely form direct synaptic connections with these afferent terminals (Bellono et al., 2017; Kaelberer et al., 2018), and different hormones can be packaged into distinct vesicle pools within the same EEC (Fothergill et al., 2017; Fothergill and Furness, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Different hormones can be packaged into distinct vesicle pools within the same EEC.
source: Some EECs likely form direct synaptic connections with these afferent terminals (Bellono et al., 2017; Kaelberer et al., 2018), and different hormones can be packaged into distinct vesicle pools within the same EEC (Fothergill et al., 2017; Fothergill and Furness, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The spatial and functional organization of EECs creates potential mechanisms for the same hormone to have different effects depending on where it is released.
source: This spatial and functional organization of EECs creates potential mechanisms for the same hormone to have different effects depending on where it is released.
evidence: This is an inference from the known organization of EECs.

claim: Direct stimulation of CckCre cells both inhibits feeding and produces robust conditioned flavor preference.
source: For example, we found that direct stimulation of CckCre cells both inhibits feeding and produces robust conditioned flavor preference (Figure 4I), despite the fact that systemic injection of many of the individual hormones produced by these cells induces aversion at doses that inhibit food intake (Chelikani et al., 2006; Deutsch and Hardy, 1977; Ervin et al., 1995a; Ervin et al., 1984; Halatchev and Cone, 2005; Kanoski et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 4, contrasted with prior work cited.

claim: Systemic injection of many of the individual hormones produced by CckCre cells induces aversion at doses that inhibit food intake.
source: For example, we found that direct stimulation of CckCre cells both inhibits feeding and produces robust conditioned flavor preference (Figure 4I), despite the fact that systemic injection of many of the individual hormones produced by these cells induces aversion at doses that inhibit food intake (Chelikani et al., 2006; Deutsch and Hardy, 1977; Ervin et al., 1995a; Ervin et al., 1984; Halatchev and Cone, 2005; Kanoski et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: A PYY receptor antagonist blocked the anorexia produced by stimulation of CckCre cells but not Tac1Cre cells, even though PYY was expressed by subsets of both EECs.
source: We also found that the same hormone produced by different EECs can have different functions. For example, a PYY receptor antagonist blocked the anorexia produced by stimulation of CckCre cells but not Tac1Cre cells, even though PYY was expressed by subsets of both EECs (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: A 5-HT3R antagonist blocked the anorectic effect of stimulating Tac1Cre but not CckCre EECs, although many CckCre EECs also produce 5-HT.
source: Conversely, a 5-HT3R antagonist blocked the anorectic effect of stimulating Tac1Cre but not CckCre EECs (Figure 5A and B), although many CckCre EECs also produce 5-HT (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a finding from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: EEC signaling is highly organized within the lamina propria, such that neurotransmitters released by EEC subtypes are funneled to specific sensory pathways.
source: These observations are consistent with the idea that EEC signaling is highly organized within the lamina propria, such that neurotransmitters released by EEC subtypes are funneled to specific sensory pathways.
evidence: This is an inference from the differential effects of receptor antagonists.

claim: Post-ingestive signals shape our decisions about what to eat and can override innate preferences.
source: Post-ingestive signals shape our decisions about what to eat and can override innate preferences, such that animals learn to prefer bitter foods that are nutritious and avoid sweet substances that are toxic (Kern et al., 1993; Lin et al., 2017; Myers and Sclafani, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Animals learn to prefer bitter foods that are nutritious and avoid sweet substances that are toxic.
source: Post-ingestive signals shape our decisions about what to eat and can override innate preferences, such that animals learn to prefer bitter foods that are nutritious and avoid sweet substances that are toxic (Kern et al., 1993; Lin et al., 2017; Myers and Sclafani, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The gut epithelium is the interface between ingested food and the body.
source: The gut epithelium is the interface between ingested food and the body and is poised to provide feedback about ingested food that drives learning.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Stimulation of two different EEC types was sufficient to drive either food preference or aversion.
source: The major finding from these experiments was that stimulation of two different EEC types was sufficient to drive either food preference or aversion, and that the effects of these cells were mediated by parallel gut-brain pathways that involve distinct hormones and afferent nerves.
evidence: This is a summary of the major findings from Figures 4-6.

claim: The effects of different EEC types on food preference and aversion were mediated by parallel gut-brain pathways that involve distinct hormones and afferent nerves.
source: The major finding from these experiments was that stimulation of two different EEC types was sufficient to drive either food preference or aversion, and that the effects of these cells were mediated by parallel gut-brain pathways that involve distinct hormones and afferent nerves.
evidence: This is a summary of the major findings from Figures 4-6.

claim: Prior work has shown that CCK injections can induce flavor preference at low doses that do not affect feeding.
source: Of note, prior work has shown that CCK injections can induce flavor preference at low doses that do not affect feeding (Pérez and Sclafani, 1991) and aversion at higher doses (Deutsch and Hardy, 1977; Ervin et al., 1995a; Ervin et al., 1995b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: CCK injections can induce aversion at higher doses.
source: Of note, prior work has shown that CCK injections can induce flavor preference at low doses that do not affect feeding (Pérez and Sclafani, 1991) and aversion at higher doses (Deutsch and Hardy, 1977; Ervin et al., 1995a; Ervin et al., 1995b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The effect of CckCre cells on satiety and food preference required intact vagal afferents, but not spinal afferents.
source: The effect of CckCre cells on satiety and food preference required intact vagal afferents, but not spinal afferents, which is consistent with an extensive literature showing that the vagus nerve mediates many of CCK's effects (Joyner et al., 1993; Raybould, 2007; Ritter and Ladenheim, 1985; Smith et al., 1981; Smith et al., 1985).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 6, consistent with prior work cited.

claim: The vagus nerve mediates many of CCK's effects.
source: The effect of CckCre cells on satiety and food preference required intact vagal afferents, but not spinal afferents, which is consistent with an extensive literature showing that the vagus nerve mediates many of CCK's effects (Joyner et al., 1993; Raybould, 2007; Ritter and Ladenheim, 1985; Smith et al., 1981; Smith et al., 1985).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The CCKAR is expressed in multiple vagal subtypes, including IGLE mechanoreceptors that innervate the stomach (Glp1r+) and intestine (Oxtr+).
source: The CCKAR is expressed in multiple vagal subtypes, including IGLE mechanoreceptors that innervate the stomach (Glp1r+) and intestine (Oxtr+) (Bai et al., 2019; Williams et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: IGLE mechanoreceptors inhibit food intake when stimulated.
source: These IGLE subtypes inhibit food intake when stimulated (Bai et al., 2019) and are required for the reduction in feeding following CCK injection (Borgmann et al., 2021) and therefore likely contribute to the effects of CckCre EECs on food intake.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: IGLE mechanoreceptors are required for the reduction in feeding following CCK injection.
source: These IGLE subtypes inhibit food intake when stimulated (Bai et al., 2019) and are required for the reduction in feeding following CCK injection (Borgmann et al., 2021) and therefore likely contribute to the effects of CckCre EECs on food intake.
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: IGLE mechanoreceptors likely contribute to the effects of CckCre EECs on food intake.
source: These IGLE subtypes inhibit food intake when stimulated (Bai et al., 2019) and are required for the reduction in feeding following CCK injection (Borgmann et al., 2021) and therefore likely contribute to the effects of CckCre EECs on food intake.
evidence: This is an inference from prior work and the current findings.

claim: Stimulation of all gut-innervating vagal afferents is reinforcing.
source: It is less clear which vagal cells mediate CCK's effects on flavor preference, although stimulation of all gut-innervating vagal afferents is reinforcing (Han et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Vip+/Uts2b+ vagal neurons innervate the intestinal mucosa and express high levels of CCKAR but do not inhibit food intake when stimulated.
source: One plausible candidate is the Vip+/Uts2b+vagal neurons that innervate the intestinal mucosa and express high levels of CCKAR but do not inhibit food intake when stimulated (Bai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as speculation with citation to prior work.

claim: Peripheral 5-HT has been implicated in numerous processes including GI motility, secretion, vasoconstriction, bone growth, inflammation, visceral malaise, metabolism, and appetite.
source: Peripheral 5-HT has been implicated in numerous processes including GI motility, secretion, vasoconstriction, bone growth, inflammation, visceral malaise, metabolism, and appetite (Mawe and Hoffman, 2013; Spohn and Mawe, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Enterochromaffin cells are the major source of 5-HT in the gut.
source: Enterochromaffin cells are the major source of 5-HT in the gut, and we found that direct stimulation of Tac1Cre-labeled enterochromaffin cells acutely inhibited food intake and caused dramatic CTA.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The CTA induced by enterochromaffin cells could be fully prevented only by simultaneously blocking receptors for two hormones produced by these cells during training (5-HT3R and TACR1).
source: The inhibition of food intake required 5-HT signaling, whereas the CTA could be fully prevented only by simultaneously blocking receptors for two hormones produced by these cells during training (5-HT3R and TACR1).
evidence: This is a finding from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Some biological functions of EECs are encoded in their ability to release cocktails of hormones with redundant functions.
source: This is consistent with the hypothesis that some biological functions of EECs are encoded in their ability to release cocktails of hormones with redundant functions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings from the study.

claim: Intestinal serotonin can activate both vagal and spinal pathways.
source: Intestinal serotonin can activate both vagal and spinal pathways, but we found that only spinal afferents were required for the reduction in food intake and CTA triggered by stimulation of enterochromaffin cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, contrasted with the current findings.

claim: Only spinal afferents were required for the reduction in food intake and CTA triggered by stimulation of enterochromaffin cells.
source: Intestinal serotonin can activate both vagal and spinal pathways, but we found that only spinal afferents were required for the reduction in food intake and CTA triggered by stimulation of enterochromaffin cells.
evidence: This is a finding from vagotomy and RTX experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Enterochromaffin cell effects may be mediated by 5-HT3R-expressing spinal afferents that innervate the distal intestine.
source: This may be mediated by 5-HT3R-expressing spinal afferents that innervate the distal intestine (Hockley et al., 2019), are functionally coupled to enterochromaffin cells (Bellono et al., 2017), and are poised to transmit aversive visceral signals (such as abdominal pain) that are sensitive to 5-HT3R antagonists (Ford et al., 2009; Gebhart and Bielefeldt, 2016).
evidence: This is speculation based on prior work cited.

claim: 5-HT3R-expressing spinal afferents are functionally coupled to enterochromaffin cells.
source: This may be mediated by 5-HT3R-expressing spinal afferents that innervate the distal intestine (Hockley et al., 2019), are functionally coupled to enterochromaffin cells (Bellono et al., 2017), and are poised to transmit aversive visceral signals (such as abdominal pain) that are sensitive to 5-HT3R antagonists (Ford et al., 2009; Gebhart and Bielefeldt, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: 5-HT3R-expressing spinal afferents are poised to transmit aversive visceral signals (such as abdominal pain) that are sensitive to 5-HT3R antagonists.
source: This may be mediated by 5-HT3R-expressing spinal afferents that innervate the distal intestine (Hockley et al., 2019), are functionally coupled to enterochromaffin cells (Bellono et al., 2017), and are poised to transmit aversive visceral signals (such as abdominal pain) that are sensitive to 5-HT3R antagonists (Ford et al., 2009; Gebhart and Bielefeldt, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Many vagal sensory neurons also express 5-HT3Rs.
source: Of note, many vagal sensory neurons also express 5-HT3Rs, and our findings do not rule out a role for those cells in nausea (Babic and Browning, 2014) or non-aversive satiety (Savastano and Covasa, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The findings do not rule out a role for vagal 5-HT3R+ neurons in nausea or non-aversive satiety.
source: Of note, many vagal sensory neurons also express 5-HT3Rs, and our findings do not rule out a role for those cells in nausea (Babic and Browning, 2014) or non-aversive satiety (Savastano and Covasa, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the current findings with citations.
